name: Niels Henrik Abel
milestone_by_age_26: Published the first complete proof of the impossibility of solving the general quintic equation in radicals (Abel-Ruffini theorem) in 1824 at age 21, and contributed seven articles to the first volume of Crelle's Journal in 1826.
early_history_summary: Abel's mathematical talent was discovered by his teacher Bernt Michael Holmboe at the Cathedral School in Christiania in 1818. He entered the Royal Frederick University in 1821 already the most knowledgeable mathematician in Norway, and by 1823 had proved the impossibility of solving the quintic equation in radicals.
family_context_summary: Father was a pastor with degrees in theology and philology. Family fell into poverty after father's death in 1820. Mother was reportedly an alcoholic who took little interest in the children's upbringing.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a pastor with academic training but no mathematical background. No family domain advantage in mathematics.
primary_early_advantage_tags: dedicated mentor, poverty-driven urgency, exceptional mathematical talent, cathedral school
evidence_summary: Abel's mathematical genius was discovered by his teacher Holmboe at age 16, who gave him private lessons and guided him to advanced mathematical literature. Despite growing up in poverty and losing his father at 18, Abel proved the impossibility of solving the quintic equation by age 21 and published it in 1824. His work was recognized by leading mathematicians including Crelle, who published seven of Abel's articles in the first volume of his journal. Abel died at 26 from tuberculosis, but his contributions reshaped multiple areas of mathematics.

name: Brian Kernighan
milestone_by_age_26: K&R C was published in 1978 when Kernighan was 36, not 26. His PhD was completed in 1969 at age 27. No material milestone by age 26 found; he was still a graduate student at Princeton.

name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
milestone_by_age_26: Published his first formal paper 'Some Properties of Bernoulli's Numbers' in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society in 1911 at age 23, and wrote the famous letter to G.H. Hardy on 16 January 1913 at age 25 containing groundbreaking theorems that Hardy recognized as extraordinary.
early_history_summary: A self-taught mathematical prodigy from a poor family in Kumbakonam, India, Ramanujan independently developed deep mathematical results in isolation. He obtained Carr's Synopsis of 5,000 theorems at age 16 and independently investigated Bernoulli numbers. After failing college exams due to focusing only on mathematics, he worked as a clerk while continuing research, eventually publishing in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society and writing to Hardy.
family_context_summary: Father worked as a clerk in a sari shop. Mother was a housewife who sang at a local temple. Family lived in a small traditional home in Kumbakonam in extreme poverty.
parent_family_domain_summary: No mathematical background in family. Father was a sari shop clerk. Mother was a housewife. No domain advantage transferred.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught prodigy, extreme poverty, isolation, obsessive mathematical focus
evidence_summary: Ramanujan was a self-taught mathematical genius who grew up in extreme poverty in colonial India with no access to formal mathematical training or the mathematical establishment. He independently developed thousands of results working in isolation, using only Carr's Synopsis as a starting point. His first paper was published in 1911 in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society, and his famous 1913 letter to Hardy containing groundbreaking theorems led to his invitation to Cambridge. Hardy described the theorems as ones that 'defeated me completely.' Ramanujan's achievements came despite, not because of, his early circumstances.

name: Ann Miura-Ko
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Floodgate at age 35-36 in 2008. Before that, she was an undergrad at Yale, worked at McKinsey and Charles River Ventures, and was a PhD student at Stanford. No material milestone by age 26 found.

name: G.H. Hardy
milestone_by_age_26: Elected fellow of Trinity College in 1900 at age 23 and won Smith's Prize in 1901, but his early papers were problem solutions in the Educational Times and a competent but not seminal integration paper. His most influential work (collaboration with Littlewood from 1911, work with Ramanujan 1913-1920, 'A Course of Pure Mathematics' 1908) all came after age 26. No seminal publication or significant discovery by age 26.

name: Chad Hurley
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded YouTube in 2005 at age 28. Before that, he worked at PayPal as a graphic designer (1999-2002) and designed the PayPal logo. By age 26 he was a freelance design consultant. No material milestone by age 26 found.

name: Paul Allen
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Microsoft with Bill Gates in 1975 at age 22 and co-developed Altair BASIC, the first product of the company that would pioneer the personal computer revolution.
early_history_summary: Allen attended Lakeside School, a prestigious private school in Seattle, where he met Bill Gates and developed programming skills on Teletype terminals. He attended Washington State University but dropped out to work at Honeywell in Boston, then convinced Gates to drop out of Harvard to found Microsoft after seeing the Altair 8800 on the cover of Popular Electronics.
family_context_summary: Father was associate director of University of Washington Libraries. Mother was a fourth-grade teacher. Parents sent him to the prestigious Lakeside School, which was expensive, and credited their love of learning for stimulating his interests.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a librarian at a university, mother was a teacher. No direct tech domain expertise, but academic/educational environment. Parents valued learning and sent him to an elite private school.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Lakeside School, rare computer access, Bill Gates partnership, personal computer revolution
evidence_summary: Allen's path to co-founding Microsoft was shaped by his attendance at Lakeside School, a prestigious private school that provided rare access to Teletype terminals and time-sharing computers. There he met Bill Gates, forming a partnership that would define the personal computer era. His father, a university librarian, and mother, a teacher, valued learning and could afford the expensive school. Allen spotted the Altair 8800 on Popular Electronics and convinced Gates to develop BASIC for it, leading to the founding of Microsoft in 1975 when Allen was 22.

name: David Hilbert
milestone_by_age_26: Proved the Hilbert Basis Theorem in 1888 at age 26, solving Gordan's Problem in invariant theory with a revolutionary non-constructive existence proof that Klein called 'the most important work on general algebra that the Annalen has ever published.'
early_history_summary: Hilbert studied at the University of Königsberg from 1880, where he formed close friendships with Hermann Minkowski and Adolf Hurwitz that profoundly influenced his mathematical development. He completed his PhD under Ferdinand von Lindemann in 1885 and remained at Königsberg as a Privatdozent from 1886. In 1888, he proved his famous Basis Theorem, solving a problem that had stumped mathematicians for twenty years.
family_context_summary: Father Otto was a county judge who taught Prussian virtues. Mother Maria had interests in philosophy, astronomy, and prime numbers. Paternal grandfather was also a judge and Geheimrat.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother had interest in philosophy, astronomy, and prime numbers, which may have influenced Hilbert's mathematical interests. Father was a judge with no mathematical background but provided a stable middle-class academic environment.
primary_early_advantage_tags: University of Königsberg, Minkowski friendship, Hurwitz mentorship, German mathematical tradition
evidence_summary: Hilbert's mathematical development was shaped by the rich intellectual environment at the University of Königsberg, where he formed lifelong friendships with Minkowski and Hurwitz that drove his mathematical growth. His mother's interest in prime numbers and philosophy may have provided early intellectual exposure. By 1888, at age 26, he proved the Basis Theorem, solving Gordan's Problem with a revolutionary non-constructive approach that initially drew criticism from Gordan but was championed by Klein. His father's position as a judge provided a stable middle-class background that supported his academic career.

name: Soichiro Honda
milestone_by_age_26: Started his own auto repair business at age 22 in 1928, but this was a small repair shop, not a major company. Founded Honda Motor Co. in 1948 at age 42. No material milestone by age 26 found.

name: Bernhard Riemann
milestone_by_age_26: Completed his doctoral thesis in 1851 at age 25, introducing the concept of Riemann surfaces, which became a foundational concept in complex analysis. The thesis was described as 'one of the most remarkable pieces of original work to appear in a doctoral thesis.'
early_history_summary: Riemann was educated by his father, a poor Lutheran pastor, until age 10, then attended schools in Hannover and Lüneburg. He studied at the University of Göttingen and University of Berlin, where he was influenced by Gauss, Dirichlet, Jacobi, and Eisenstein. He developed the general theory of complex variables during his time in Berlin, which formed the basis of his groundbreaking 1851 thesis.
family_context_summary: Father was a poor Lutheran pastor who fought in the Napoleonic Wars. Mother died when Riemann was young. Family was poor, and Riemann was shy and suffered from homesickness and health issues.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a Lutheran pastor who initially encouraged Riemann to study theology. No mathematical background in family, but father provided basic education and eventually permitted Riemann to switch to mathematics.
primary_early_advantage_tags: University of Göttingen, University of Berlin, Gauss, Dirichlet, Jacobi, poor family, mathematical prodigy
evidence_summary: Riemann grew up in a poor pastor's family in rural Germany but gained access to the leading mathematical centers of his era through the University of Göttingen (where he studied under Gauss) and the University of Berlin (where he was influenced by Dirichlet, Jacobi, and Eisenstein). His extraordinary mathematical talent was evident early - he read Legendre's 900-page number theory book in six days as a teenager. His 1851 doctoral thesis introducing Riemann surfaces was described as one of the most remarkable pieces of original work in a doctoral thesis, and it laid the groundwork for modern complex analysis.

name: Yvon Chouinard
category: Climbing gear manufacturer and outdoor apparel entrepreneur
milestone_by_age_26: Started making climbing pitons in 1957 at age 18-19 and selling them from his car, but Chouinard Equipment Ltd. was not formally established until around 1966 at age 27-28. Founded Patagonia in 1973 at age 34. No material milestone by age 26 found.

name: Évariste Galois
milestone_by_age_26: Published his first mathematical article on continued fractions in April 1829 at age 17, and published three foundational papers in 1830 at age 18-19 that laid the groundwork for Galois theory and group theory, including the first articulation of the concept of a finite field.
early_history_summary: Galois was educated at home by his mother until age 12, then attended the Collège Royal de Louis-le-Grand. His mathematical ability blossomed when he began studying Legendre's geometry and other advanced works. He submitted papers to the Académie des Sciences as a teenager, but they were lost or rejected by Cauchy and Fourier. Despite these setbacks, he published three important papers in 1830.
family_context_summary: Father Nicolas-Gabriel Galois was an important citizen and mayor of Bourg-la-Reine. Mother Adélaïde-Marie was well educated in philosophy, classical literature, and religion, and served as Galois's sole teacher until age 12. No mathematical ability in the family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother was well educated in philosophy and classical literature but had no mathematical background. Father was a mayor and important community figure but not a mathematician. No mathematical domain advantage transferred.
primary_early_advantage_tags: mathematical prodigy, Collège Louis-le-Grand, Paris, academic rejection, political turmoil, father's suicide
evidence_summary: Galois was a mathematical prodigy whose mother provided a strong classical education at home until age 12. At the Collège Louis-le-Grand, his mathematical talent blossomed, and by his late teens he had solved the 350-year-old problem of determining when a polynomial is solvable by radicals. Despite having his major memoir lost by Cauchy and Fourier, he published three foundational papers in 1830 that laid the groundwork for Galois theory and group theory. His career was marked by severe adversity: his father's suicide, repeated academic rejections, political activism, imprisonment, and his death in a duel at age 20.
